title: Which Tag Lied?

narrative.intro: Three releases went out this month, one after another: v1.0.0, v1.0.1, v1.0.2. All signed, all in order, nothing about the sequence itself looks wrong. A downstream team just filed a bug report: they upgraded from v1.0.1 to v1.0.2 expecting a routine patch, like the version number promised, and it broke their integration. You go back and read what each tagged commit actually says it is.
narrative.correctDebrief: Correct - v1.0.2's own commit message starts with "feat!:", the Conventional Commits marker for a breaking change. That should have been v2.0.0, not a PATCH bump. Nothing else about the release looked wrong - it was signed, it shipped in order, the tag sequence looked perfectly ordinary. That's the whole failure mode Build & Release Management exists to prevent: without something actually gating "does this tag's version number match what the commit itself claims to be," a breaking change can wear a patch release's clothes all the way to production, and the first person to find out is a downstream consumer who trusted the number.
narrative.incorrectDebrief: Don't just check whether the tags are signed and in order - read what each commit message actually says about the size of the change, and compare that to the version bump its tag claims. One of these three doesn't match.

c3.message: feat!: replace session cookies with JWT, breaking all existing sessions

prompt: Which tagged release doesn't actually match what its own commit says it is?

options.label: None - all three are labeled correctly
